docs.title: MultiMM
docs.text:
Welcome! MultiMM is a program that turns experimental data about the genome into a 3D picture of chromatin, from a single gene up to the whole nucleus. It is built on OpenMM, a fast simulation engine, and it is multiscale: one model can describe several levels of chromatin organisation at once, and you decide which ones to switch on.

You do not need to be a physicist to use it. If you are a biologist, you can run it with a short settings file and some data. If you are curious about how it works, the documentation explains every ingredient step by step, with pictures, and every new symbol is introduced when it first appears. It is written to be readable in your first year of physics, biology or computer science.

docs.title: The main idea
docs.text:
Chromatin is a very long string of DNA and proteins, a polymer. Imagine it as a necklace of \(N\) beads, where each bead stands for a stretch of the genome (for example 10 kb, that is 10 000 DNA letters). The question is: how is this necklace folded in 3D? We answer it by giving the necklace an energy that is low when the folding agrees with the experiments and high when it does not, and then letting the computer find the shape with the lowest energy:

\[ E = E_\text{backbone} + E_\text{data} + E_\text{nucleus}, \]

built from three kinds of ingredients:

  • Backbone (\(E_\text{backbone}\)): keeps the chain connected, stiff and self-avoiding. This part needs no data.
  • Data-driven forces (\(E_\text{data}\)): translate experimental measurements into attractions and restraints. Chromatin loops (ChIA-PET, HiChIP, Hi-C loop calls), A/B compartments, or a raw Hi-C contact matrix each become a force on the beads.
  • Nuclear environment (\(E_\text{nucleus}\)): a spherical container, anchoring of B-compartment chromatin to the nuclear lamina, chromosome territories and nucleolar positioning. These matter for chromosome- and genome-scale runs.

Each term is a separate switch in the configuration file, so the same program covers very different questions with very different input data.

Two design choices make it fast:

  1. GPU parallelisation through OpenMM (CUDA or OpenCL), with a CPU fallback.
  2. A Hilbert curve as the starting conformation. A Hilbert curve is a space-filling curve that already folds the chain into a compact, territory-like shape in which genomic neighbours are also spatial neighbours. The optimiser therefore starts close to a sensible answer instead of from a random coil (see Initial structure).

docs.title: What can I model?
docs.text:
Choose the level that matches your question; MultiMM sets sensible defaults for it.

Level Scope Typical forces GENE A gene and its flanking region backbone + loops or Hi-C force REGION A user-defined interval (a TAD, a locus, a few Mb) backbone + loops or Hi-C force (+ compartments) CHROM A whole chromosome backbone + loops/Hi-C + compartments GW All chromosomes in one nucleus full force field, including nucleus and lamina

Optionally, a finished structure can be refined to nucleosome resolution using ATAC-seq (see Advanced options).

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• New here? Start with Installation, then try the quick example in the project README.
  • Want to understand what the program computes? Read The Model. Every force is explained with its equation and with the exact choices MultiMM makes.
  • Ready to run your own data? Go to the Reference: how to run, how to write a config file, and a table of every argument.

Scope

MultiMM is designed for human genome data. Other organisms may work with additional modifications, but full support is not guaranteed. It accepts input derived from Hi-C, single-cell Hi-C, ChIA-PET and HiChIP experiments. Default parameters are tuned for population-average Hi-C; please check convergence on your own data.

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text:
MultiMM started with a simple request. My friends in the lab are biologists. They had beautiful Hi-C maps, loop calls and compartment tracks, and they wanted one thing: to see what the genome looks like in 3D, quickly, without first having to learn polymer physics or read a pile of papers about force fields.

That request stayed with me. Over the years I have built several programs for 3D chromatin modelling. Each of them was, in the end, a model: a clever idea that works well for one question, at one scale, for the person who wrote it. MultiMM is meant to be something different. It is a tool, not just a model.

docs.title: What I wanted to build
docs.text:
My goal was a really user-friendly piece of software. In practice, that means a few things.

  • You should not need to know the physics to get a result. Choose a level (a gene, a region, a chromosome or the whole genome), point MultiMM to your data, and run it. The defaults are chosen so that this works.
  • You should be able to model any chromatin scale. The same program builds a 1000-bead picture of one gene and its surroundings, and a 200 000-bead picture of the entire nucleus. You do not switch software when your question grows.
  • Everything should be in one place. All the forces (loops, compartments, Hi-C restraints, the nuclear envelope and more) and all their alternative forms are available as options. You can use a single one or combine them as you like.
  • It should be usable in different ways. You can run it with one command, drive it from a small configuration file, or call it from your own Python code. It runs models, but it also checks them against your data and produces figures, so the whole path from data to picture is covered.

docs.title: Physics is a helper, not a barrier
docs.text:
Chromatin modelling is, in a good sense, phenomenological. We do not simulate every atom. We describe chromatin as a chain of beads and add simple rules that capture what the experiments show: beads cannot overlap, loops hold two points together, active and inactive regions like to meet their own kind. You do not need deep mathematics to use such rules, and many ideas in this documentation are as simple as "a spring" or "a magnet".

At the same time, I know that many people are scared of modelling. It looks like a locked room that only physicists can enter. I would like this documentation, and the software itself, to be a door that is open: if you are curious, you can go deeper and see exactly what each term does, with equations and pictures; if you only need a structure for your figure, you can stay on the surface and still get a sound result.

If you are a biologist, I hope MultiMM lets you test your ideas about genome folding in an afternoon. If you are a physicist or a computer scientist, I hope the Model chapter gives you everything you need to understand, question and extend it.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Getting started takes a few minutes and a few commands. If you have never installed a Python package, do not worry: just copy the lines below into a terminal one by one.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • Linux is the primary, tested platform (Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat). macOS also works, but without CUDA. Windows is not recommended (the pyBigWig dependency does not support it).
  • A GPU is optional but strongly recommended for anything larger than a few thousand beads. MultiMM uses OpenMM, which supports NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA and many GPUs through OpenCL. Without a GPU the CPU platform is used.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install MultiMM

Reading .hic Hi-C files needs one optional package, hic-straw, which has to compile some C++ code and can be fussy to install. It is therefore not installed by default; if you use .hic files, add it with

pip install "MultiMM[hic]"

.cool and .mcool files need nothing extra.

Using a virtual environment keeps the many scientific dependencies separate from your system Python:

python -m venv multimm-env
source multimm-env/bin/activate
pip install MultiMM

Check that the command-line tool is available:

MultiMM --help

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install it in editable mode if you want to modify the code:

git clone https://github.com/SFGLab/MultiMM.git
cd MultiMM
pip install -e .

The project also ships a uv.lock file, so uv users can instead run uv sync inside the cloned folder to get exactly the dependency versions the project was developed with.

docs.title: Choosing a compute platform
docs.text:
OpenMM selects the hardware through the PLATFORM setting in the config file (see Arguments):

PLATFORM Hardware When to use CUDA NVIDIA GPU Fastest option if you have an NVIDIA card and drivers OpenCL Most GPUs (and CPUs) Good general choice on GPUs without CUDA CPU CPU cores Small systems; set CPU_THREADS to control parallelism Reference Single CPU thread Debugging only, very slow

If the requested GPU platform is not found, MultiMM prints a message and falls back to the CPU. To see which platforms your OpenMM installation provides, run:

python -m openmm.testInstallation

docs.title: Example data
docs.text: A small example dataset (GM12878 Hi-C from Rao et al., CALDER subcompartments and ENCODE ATAC-seq) is available on Google Drive. The examples/ folder of the repository holds ready-to-edit configuration files for the common scenarios (genome-wide, a single region, single-cell data, and the Hi-C force).

docs.title: Installing the documentation tools
docs.text:
To build this documentation locally:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve        # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000

docs.title: The Model: overview
docs.text: This chapter explains what MultiMM computes, in small steps. We describe the energy of the chromatin chain, term by term, and say for each term which biological fact it stands for and how it is built from data. Equations are there for those who want them, but each one comes with a sentence in plain words, so you can read the text even if you skip the formulas. Boxes titled In MultiMM state exactly what the program does and which settings control it. To run the program and to see the full list of settings, go to the Reference.

docs.title: A few words you will meet
docs.text: Word Meaning Bead One piece of the chain, standing for a stretch of the genome. Energy A number that tells how "unhappy" a shape is. Nature, and our program, prefer low energy. Force The push or pull that follows from an energy: a bead moves in the direction that lowers the energy. A force field is the whole collection of such terms. Minimisation Moving the beads step by step downhill in energy until no small move helps. \(k_BT\) The energy scale of thermal jiggling (at body temperature about 2.6 kJ/mol). An interaction much weaker than this is washed out, a much stronger one is felt. Hi-C An experiment that counts how often pairs of genome regions touch each other in the nucleus. Loop, TAD, compartment Three levels of folding seen in Hi-C: two points held together (loop), a self-contacting domain (TAD), and large active (A) or inactive (B) regions that gather with their own kind (compartments). Kernel A formula that says how a quantity (like attraction) changes with distance. We often offer several, and say which is the default.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text: Data from a 3C-type experiment (loops, compartments, or the raw contact matrix) are reduced to a small set of per-bead quantities. These are combined with an initial structure and a configuration file, and OpenMM then minimises the energy (and optionally runs molecular dynamics). ATAC-seq enters only at the end, to refine the finished structure to nucleosome resolution.

docs.title: How the components connect
docs.text: Read the diagram from top to bottom. Everything in the second row is a number attached to beads or pairs of beads, so the rest of this chapter works with exactly those objects.

docs.title: The total energy
docs.text:
The chromatin chain has \(N\) beads at positions \(\mathbf{r}_1,\dots,\mathbf{r}_N\). The distance between beads \(i\) and \(j\) is \(r_{ij}=\lVert\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j\rVert\). MultiMM minimises

\[ E = E_\text{bond} + E_\text{angle} + E_\text{EV} + E_\text{loop} + E_\text{Hi-C} + E_\text{comp} + E_\text{sub} + E_\text{chrom} + E_\text{container} + E_\text{lamina} + E_\text{central}. \]

Each term answers one biological question:

Term Question it answers Page Switch in the config file \(E_\text{bond}\) Which beads are neighbours along the chain? Backbone POL_USE_HARMONIC_BOND \(E_\text{angle}\) How stiff is the chromatin fibre? Backbone POL_USE_HARMONIC_ANGLE \(E_\text{EV}\) Beads cannot overlap Backbone EV_USE_EXCLUDED_VOLUME \(E_\text{loop}\) Which distant beads are held together by loops? Loops LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND \(E_\text{Hi-C}\) Which pairs are in contact, and how strongly? Hi-C force HIC_USE_FORCE \(E_\text{comp}\) Do A and B chromatin separate? Compartments COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS \(E_\text{sub}\) Do A1, A2, B1, B2 separate further? Compartments SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS \(E_\text{chrom}\) Does each chromosome form its own territory? Compartments CHB_USE_CHROMOSOMAL_BLOCKS \(E_\text{container}\) Where are the walls of the nucleus? Nuclear envelope and lamina SC_USE_SPHERICAL_CONTAINER \(E_\text{lamina}\) Is B chromatin pulled to the periphery? Nuclear envelope and lamina IBL_USE_B_LAMINA_INTERACTION \(E_\text{central}\) Do small chromosomes sit near the centre? Nuclear envelope and lamina CF_USE_CENTRAL_FORCE

A term whose switch is off simply does not exist in the energy.

In MultiMM

Every term is added to the OpenMM System as its own force object and is placed in its own force group. That is why MultiMM can plot the energy of each term separately over a molecular dynamics run (plots/energy_components.png), which is the quickest way to see which force is driving the structure.

Combinations that are checked at start-up

  • Lamina anchoring needs compartment labels and an active compartment (or subcompartment) force.
  • A compartment force needs a COMPARTMENT_PATH (or HIC_BLOCK_COPOLYMER, see Hi-C force).
  • Loop bonds need a LOOPS_PATH; the Hi-C force needs a HIC_PATH.
  • Using loops, Hi-C and compartments together is allowed but triggers a warning, because the three can over-constrain the same structure.

docs.title: The simulation protocol
docs.text:
1. Build. Create the initial structure (Initial structure), load the data, convert it to per-bead quantities, and assemble the force field.
  2. Minimise. OpenMM's minimizeEnergy moves the beads to the nearest local minimum of \(E\). This produces MultiMM_minimized.cif and is the main result.
  3. Relax (optional, SIM_RUN_MD). Molecular dynamics at temperature \(T\) with a Langevin thermostat, starting from Maxwell–Boltzmann velocities. It samples fluctuations around the minimum and writes one structure per saved frame. See Minimisation and dynamics for what this means and for the integrators.
  4. Validate and post-process. Compare the model with the input data (Hi-C correlations, loop distances, compartment clustering), run quality checks, make plots, and optionally add nucleosomes.

A note on strategy: because the Hilbert-curve start is already compact and ordered, minimisation alone is usually enough for large systems, while molecular dynamics is most useful for small regions where you want an ensemble of conformations.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(N\) Number of beads (N_BEADS) \(i,\,j\) Bead indices, \(1\le i,j\le N\) \(r_{ij}\) Distance between beads \(i\) and \(j\) \(b_0\) Bond length, the basic length unit (POL_HARMONIC_BOND_R0) \(k_BT\) Thermal energy, \(\approx 2.58\) kJ/mol at 310 K \(s_i\) Compartment state of bead \(i\) (\(\pm1,\pm2\), or \(0\) if unknown) \(\chi_i\) Chromosome label of bead \(i\) \(c_{ij}\) Hi-C contact strength between beads \(i\) and \(j\), scaled to \([0,1]\) \(\delta(a,b)\) Kronecker delta: 1 if \(a=b\), otherwise 0 \(\Theta(x)\) Step function: 1 for \(x>0\), otherwise 0 \(R_1,\,R_2\) Inner and outer radius of the nuclear shell

All lengths, energies and scales are defined in Units and scales.

docs.title: Advanced options
docs.text: This page collects options that change what is modelled or how the result is sampled, rather than the energy terms themselves.

docs.title: Modelling levels
docs.text:
MODELLING_LEVEL is a shortcut that sets many parameters at once for a typical scale. The preset is applied after the configuration is read and overwrites the listed parameters (the changes are printed at the start of the run). Everything else keeps your value.

Level Typical use Beads Container Compartment force B-lamina MD GENE one gene and its surroundings 1000 off off off on, 10 000 steps REGION (or LOC) a TAD-scale or Mb-scale region 5000 off on if COMPARTMENT_PATH is given off on, 10 000 steps CHROM (or CHROMOSOME) a whole chromosome 20 000 off on if COMPARTMENT_PATH is given off on, 10 000 steps GW (or GENOME) the whole genome 200 000 on on if COMPARTMENT_PATH is given on if COMPARTMENT_PATH is given off

All presets also switch off the chromosome blocks, the subcompartment force and the central force. CHROM additionally sets LOC_START = 1 and LOC_END to the length of CHROM. Leave MODELLING_LEVEL empty to configure everything yourself.

Presets override your settings

A preset overwrites, for example, N_BEADS. If you want 20 000 beads on a region, do not use a level; set the parameters directly.

docs.title: Gene modelling
docs.text:
With MODELLING_LEVEL = GENE, the modelled region is built around a gene instead of from CHROM, LOC_START and LOC_END. Give the gene by name (GENE_NAME) or by identifier (GENE_ID). Several genes can be given as a comma-separated list (for example GENE_NAME = MYC, PVT1); the region then covers all of them plus the window (they must lie on the same chromosome). If a name has several annotations, the longest one is used. its position is looked up in an annotation table (GENE_TSV; the default is a bundled hg38 annotation). The region is the gene body extended by GENE_WINDOW base pairs on each side (default 100 000), cut to N_BEADS = 1000 beads.

Every annotated gene in the modelled window (also for MODELLING_LEVEL = REGION) is mapped onto the beads and reported, not only the requested ones:

Output Content metadata/genes_in_region.tsv one row per gene: coordinates, first and last bead, whether it is a target, its radius of gyration rg (how compact the gene is in 3D) and dist_to_target (distance of its centre to the target genes) plots/genes_3d.png the structure with every gene in its own colour (targets red, the rest of the chain grey) and gene-name labels plots/genes_track.png left: gene track along the beads, with overlapping genes stacked; right: matrix of 3D distances between gene centres, showing which genes are spatial neighbours metadata/chimera_genes_coloring.cmd ChimeraX script with the same colours

The target gene alone is also highlighted in plots/structure_afterMD_gene_coloring.png and metadata/chimera_gene_coloring.cmd. Gene mode is meant to be used with local data: a loop file and/or a Hi-C map for the region.

[Main]
MODELLING_LEVEL = GENE
GENE_NAME       = MYC
GENE_WINDOW     = 200000
LOOPS_PATH      = loops.bedpe
OUT_PATH        = results/MYC

docs.title: Why an ensemble?
docs.text:
A single run gives you one structure. But a Hi-C map is not the picture of one nucleus: it is an average over millions of cells, and in each cell the chromatin is folded a little differently (loops form and dissolve, domains wobble). One model, however good, is just one possible member of that crowd. An ensemble is a set of structures, each one a plausible conformation, that together describe the variety. Use it when you care about how much the structure varies (for example the spread of the distance between two loci), or when you want to compare with a population average such as Hi-C, which is best reproduced by averaging many structures rather than looking at one.

In plain words

Think of taking many photographs of a crowd instead of one: each photo is different, but together they show what the crowd looks like. An ensemble is that stack of photos for a piece of chromatin.

docs.title: How to switch it on
docs.text:
GENERATE_ENSEMBLE = True
N_ENSEMBLE        = 20       ; number of structures (required)

N_ENSEMBLE must be set whenever GENERATE_ENSEMBLE is True; MultiMM stops with a clear message otherwise.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
MultiMM simply runs the whole pipeline \(n\) times (N_ENSEMBLE = \(n\)), one after another. Run number \(i\) (\(i=0,\dots,n-1\)) is written to its own folder run_<i>/ inside OUT_PATH (numbers are zero-padded, so run_00 … run_19), with the usual layout of outputs, and uses the random seed SHUFFLING_SEED = i. A seed is the starting number of a pseudo-random generator: the same seed always gives the same "random" choices, so every ensemble is reproducible, while different seeds give different structures.

The seed feeds every random ingredient of the model:

Random ingredient Switched on by Effect Random-walk initial structure INITIAL_STRUCTURE_TYPE = rw, confined_rw, self_avoiding_rw, ... A different starting conformation for each run Initial velocities of the beads SIM_RUN_MD with SIM_SET_INITIAL_VELOCITIES A different dynamical trajectory for each run Loops randomly removed DOWNSAMPLING_PROB < 1 Each run keeps a different random subset of loops, mimicking that not every loop is present in every cell Compartment flips COMPARTMENT_FLIP_PROB > 0 Some beads switch A ↔ B at random Compartment noise COMPARTMENT_NOISE_STD > 0 Compartment boundaries shift slightly Hi-C noise HIC_NOISE_INTENSITY > 0 The strength of each Hi-C restraint is redrawn at every saved frame Chromosome order SHUFFLE_CHROMS The order of chromosomes in a genome-wide model is permuted

The runs must be able to differ

With the default settings the initial structure is the deterministic Hilbert curve and there is no noise, so a run that only minimises the energy gives the same structure every time and an ensemble would be \(n\) identical copies. To get variety, turn on at least one ingredient from the table: a random-walk start, molecular dynamics with random initial velocities, or one of the noise options.

docs.title: Cost and tips
docs.text:
An ensemble multiplies the computing time by \(n\), so it is best for small and medium systems (a gene or a region); for a whole genome, think twice. Start with a small \(n\) (5 to 10) to check that the structures indeed differ, then increase it. Because the structures are saved as ordinary files, you can average their contact maps afterwards or measure any distance across the runs.

SHUFFLE_CHROMS randomly permutes the order of the chromosomes in a genome-wide model, which probes how much the arrangement of territories depends on the starting order.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: PLATFORM selects the OpenMM backend: CPU (default), Reference (slow, for testing), and, when available in your OpenMM installation, CUDA or OpenCL on a GPU. Large genome-wide systems need a GPU. CPU_THREADS sets the number of CPU threads. All custom nonbonded forces are given a cutoff so that they run on the GPU platforms.

docs.title: Nucleosome interpolation
docs.text:
The beads of MultiMM are coarse (kilobases). Nucleosome interpolation is an optional post-processing step that decorates the minimised structure with explicit nucleosomes, to produce an atomistic-looking fibre for visualisation. It does not change the modelled structure.

Number of nucleosomes. From an ATAC-seq signal track (ATACSEQ_PATH, a .bigWig), the log signal \(\log(a_i+10^{-6})\) is rescaled to \(\tilde a_i\in[0,1]\). The number of nucleosomes placed between bead \(i\) and \(i+1\) is proportional to this signal (a higher value gives more nucleosomes):

\[ n_i=\operatorname{round}\!\bigl(\tilde a_i\,n_\text{max}\bigr),\qquad n_\text{max}=\left\lceil \frac{1}{2\,r_\text{nuc}}\right\rceil , \]

where \(r_\text{nuc}\) is the nucleosome radius (NUC_RADIUS, 0.1) and \(n_\text{max}\) is the maximum number of nucleosomes per bead (5 for the default).

Shape. Each nucleosome is a short helix of radius \(r_\text{nuc}\), height \(r_\text{nuc}\) and 1.65 turns (the DNA wraps about 1.65 times around the histone core), drawn with POINTS_PER_NUC points (20). Successive nucleosomes are placed at equal spacing along the segment between two beads, offset sideways in a zigzag by half a linker length (\(3.45\,r_\text{nuc}/2\), randomly scaled between 0.5 and 1.5), and rotated by a constant angle PHI_NORM (\(\pi/5\)) between neighbours, which mimics the zigzag chromatin fibre.

Known issue: not functional in this release

The step cannot currently run. The modelling-level code always resets NUC_DO_INTERPOLATION to False and ATACSEQ_PATH to none, and, in addition, the call that builds the nucleosomes passes its arguments in a different order from the function signature (MAX_NUCS_PER_BEAD is also ignored: \(n_\text{max}\) is always computed from NUC_RADIUS). The output file model/MultiMM_minimized_with_nucs.cif is therefore not produced. The description above is how the method is designed to work.

In MultiMM

Key Default NUC_DO_INTERPOLATION False ATACSEQ_PATH none NUC_RADIUS 0.1 POINTS_PER_NUC 20 PHI_NORM 0.6283 (\(\pi/5\)) MAX_NUCS_PER_BEAD 4 (ignored)

docs.title: Backbone
docs.text:
The backbone is the part of the force field that needs no experimental data. It makes the beads behave like a chromatin fibre: a connected chain with some stiffness that cannot pass through itself. All other forces act on top of it.

In plain words

Think of a string of pearls. Each pearl is tied to its neighbours by a short spring (bond), the string resists sharp bending like a garden hose (angle), and no two pearls can sit in the same place (excluded volume, a kind of personal space).

docs.title: Bonds
docs.text:
Consecutive beads are connected by a harmonic spring,

\[ E_\text{bond}=\sum_{i}\frac{k_b}{2}\,\bigl(r_{i,i+1}-b_0\bigr)^2 , \]

where \(r_{i,i+1}\) is the distance between beads \(i\) and \(i+1\), \(b_0\) is the rest length and \(k_b\) the stiffness. With the defaults a bond fluctuates by only \(\sqrt{k_BT/k_b}\approx 0.003\) nm, about 3% of \(b_0\), so the chain is practically inextensible: bonds define connectivity, not elasticity. Bonds are not created across a chromosome boundary, so every chromosome is its own chain.

Why this force, and what does it model?

DNA is a continuous molecule, so neighbouring beads must stay neighbours. A stiff spring is the simplest way to say this, and a spring is also what the computer handles best: its energy is smooth and its force is easy to compute. The spring is made so stiff that the chain is practically inextensible, so it models connectivity, not stretchiness.

docs.title: Angles (stiffness)
docs.text:
Chromatin cannot bend arbitrarily sharply. Stiffness is a harmonic term on the angle \(\theta_i\) formed by three consecutive beads,

\[ E_\text{angle}=\sum_{i}\frac{k_\theta}{2}\,\bigl(\theta_i-\theta_0\bigr)^2 . \]

With \(\theta_0=\pi\) the preferred shape is a straight line and \(k_\theta\) penalises bending. Bond plus angle form a discretised worm-like chain. In the weak-bending limit its persistence length (the contour length over which the chain keeps its direction) is about

\[ \ell_p\approx b_0\,\frac{k_\theta}{k_BT}\;\approx\;39\,b_0\quad\text{for the defaults.} \]

This is only a guide, because excluded volume and the data forces also bend the chain, but it shows how to tune stiffness: doubling \(k_\theta\) roughly doubles \(\ell_p\).

Why this force, and what does it model?

Chromatin has a real thickness, so the fibre cannot pass through itself. Without this term the chain would collapse into a point, or pass through itself like a ghost, which topoisomerases and the physical fibre forbid. The angle term models the fact that a 10 nm to 30 nm fibre is not a floppy thread but resists sharp bends (the persistence length is the distance over which it keeps its direction).

docs.title: Excluded volume
docs.text:
Two beads must not occupy the same place. A repulsive, soft-core interaction acts between all pairs of beads, including chain neighbours. Two functional forms exist; both use the size \(\sigma\) (set from LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0, 0.1 nm) and the strength \(\varepsilon\).

EV_FORCE_TYPE Energy per pair Character powerlaw (default) \(\varepsilon\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{r+r_s}\right)^{n}\) Steep repulsion that grows quickly as beads approach. The small length \(r_s\) (EV_R_SMALL) keeps it finite at \(r=0\), where it equals \(\varepsilon(\sigma/r_s)^n\) (6400 kJ/mol for the defaults), so the minimiser never meets an infinity. At \(r=b_0\) it is only about 9 kJ/mol, so chain neighbours feel a mild, nearly constant offset. gaussian_core \(\varepsilon\,e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) A very soft core: finite (\(=\varepsilon\)) at full overlap and negligible beyond about \(3\sigma\). It lets beads pass through each other, which is useful when a structure is badly crowded and needs to relax. It uses neither \(n\) nor \(r_s\).

In MultiMM

Term Keys Defaults Bond POL_USE_HARMONIC_BOND, POL_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 (\(b_0\)), POL_HARMONIC_BOND_K (\(k_b\)) True, 0.1 nm, 300 000 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻² Angle POL_USE_HARMONIC_ANGLE, POL_HARMONIC_ANGLE_R0 (\(\theta_0\)), POL_HARMONIC_ANGLE_CONSTANT_K (\(k_\theta\)) True, 3.14159 radian, 100 kJ mol⁻¹ rad⁻² Excluded volume EV_USE_EXCLUDED_VOLUME, EV_FORCE_TYPE, EV_EPSILON (\(\varepsilon\)), EV_POWER (\(n\)), EV_R_SMALL (\(r_s\)) True, powerlaw, 100 kJ/mol, 6, 0.05 nm

The excluded-volume size \(\sigma\) has no key of its own: it is read from LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 (default 0.1 nm, equal to \(b_0\)). The Hi-C force also uses it as its minimum distance. Angles are omitted at chromosome boundaries.

Rule of thumb

Leave the backbone at its defaults unless you have a reason. If the structure looks too crumpled or too straight on short scales, adjust POL_HARMONIC_ANGLE_CONSTANT_K first.

docs.title: Compartments
docs.text:
Loops organise chromatin locally. At the scale of megabases to whole chromosomes, the dominant pattern in Hi-C maps is the A/B compartments: active, open chromatin (A) contacts other A regions, and inactive, compact chromatin (B) contacts other B regions, which gives the checkerboard "plaid" pattern. MultiMM reproduces this with a block-copolymer model.

In plain words

Imagine two kinds of magnets mixed along one long string. Each kind sticks to its own kind. The string folds so that the same kinds end up together, and you get an active (A) neighbourhood and an inactive (B) neighbourhood.

docs.title: The physical idea
docs.text: Picture one chain made of two kinds of beads, A and B, that attract their own kind and ignore the other. Like oil and water, the two kinds tend to separate, but because all beads belong to the same chain they cannot separate completely: the chain folds so that A segments gather in some places and B segments in others. This is microphase separation, and it explains compartments without further assumptions. B is the denser phase because it attracts itself more strongly.

docs.title: Compartment states
docs.text:
Each bead carries a state \(s_i\):

\(s_i\) Meaning From a CALDER label \(+2\) A1 A.1… \(+1\) A2 (or A without subtype) A.2… \(-1\) B1 (or B without subtype) B.1… \(-2\) B2 B.2… \(0\) unassigned (no data) no annotation

The sign tells A from B (A beads have \(s_i>0\), B beads \(s_i<0\)) and the magnitude tells the subtype. The states come from one of three sources: a CALDER .bed file (A/B plus four subcompartments), a .bw / .bigWig signal track such as a Hi-C eigenvector (the signal is centred, scaled to \([-1,1]\) and discretised; higher values become B, lower values A; A/B only), or the Hi-C matrix itself via its first principal component (Hi-C force).

docs.title: Compartment interaction
docs.text:
Beads of the same compartment attract each other. With \(\mathbb 1_A(s)=\delta(s-1)+\delta(s-2)\) and \(\mathbb 1_B(s)=\delta(s+1)+\delta(s+2)\) marking A and B beads, the energy of a pair \((i,j)\) is

\[ U_{ij}=-\Bigl[E_A\,\mathbb 1_A(s_i)\mathbb 1_A(s_j)+E_B\,\mathbb 1_B(s_i)\mathbb 1_B(s_j)\Bigr]\;g(r_{ij}), \]

where \(E_A,E_B\) are the strengths and \(g(r)\) is a range function. Three choices of \(g\) are available (COB_FORCE_TYPE). The characteristic length \(r_c=R_2/3\) is described in Units and scales.

COB_FORCE_TYPE \(g(r)\) Character gaussian (default) \(e^{-r^2/(2r_c^2)}\) Smooth and bounded: the attraction is strongest at contact and fades gradually. Gentle on the minimiser. yukawa \(e^{-r/r_c}/r\) A "screened" attraction. It is not bounded: it grows strongly at very short distance and has a longer tail than the Gaussian. Relies on excluded volume to stay finite at \(r\to0\). theta \(\Theta(r_c-r)\) (1 inside \(r_c\), 0 outside) A square well: a constant attraction for every pair closer than \(r_c\). A pure "contact" rule with a sharp edge.

In the figure, the dotted line marks \(r_c\) (the length scale of the kernels) and the dashed line marks the cutoff: beyond it, in the grey region, pairs feel no force at all. For \(N=1000\) the cutoff (\(0.5\) nm) lies at \(1.5\,r_c\). Every form is cut off at \(5b_0\) by default (0.5 nm with the default \(b_0\)), independent of \(N\), and you can change it with COB_CUTOFF (in units of \(b_0\)). The cutoff is deliberate: without it all pairs in the system would attract and large structures would collapse. Because \(r_c=R_2/3\) grows with the system, for large \(N\) (\(r_c>5b_0\), roughly \(N\gtrsim1500\)) the cutoff, not \(r_c\), sets the real range. A larger COB_CUTOFF lets like regions feel each other from further away (stronger segregation, slower runs, more risk of over-compaction); a smaller one makes the attraction purely local.

Known issue: yukawa

In the current source the Yukawa energy uses the state of the first bead twice (s1 and s1) instead of s1 and s2. A bead in a compartment therefore attracts every other bead, not only those of its own kind, so Yukawa does not segregate A from B. Use gaussian or theta for compartment modelling until this is fixed.

In MultiMM

Key Default Role COMPARTMENT_PATH none .bed (CALDER) or .bw file COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS False Enable the force (requires COMPARTMENT_PATH) COB_FORCE_TYPE gaussian Range function \(g\) COB_EA, COB_EB 1.0, 2.0 kJ/mol \(E_A\), \(E_B\) (B is stickier, hence denser) COB_CUTOFF 5.0 (in \(b_0\)) Distance beyond which the force is zero (also used by the subcompartment force)

Why this force, and what does it model?

Hi-C shows that active (A) and inactive (B) chromatin prefer their own kind, but there is no known single protein holding them together, so we model the effect: a short-range attraction between beads of the same type. The attraction is stronger for B, which makes B denser, as observed. Different kernels (Gaussian, Yukawa, step) only change how the attraction fades with distance.

docs.title: Subcompartments
docs.text:
CALDER splits each compartment into two subtypes. With SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS each of the four states attracts only itself, with its own strength:

\[ U_{ij}=-\,\varepsilon_{s_i}\,\delta(s_i,s_j)\;g(r_{ij}),\qquad \varepsilon_{+2}=E_{A1},\ \varepsilon_{+1}=E_{A2},\ \varepsilon_{-1}=E_{B1},\ \varepsilon_{-2}=E_{B2}, \]

where \(\delta(s_i,s_j)\) is 1 if the two states are equal and 0 otherwise. The default energies \(1.0,\ 1.33,\ 1.66,\ 2.0\) kJ/mol increase from the most open to the most compact subtype, giving a finer microphase separation inside A and B. The three range functions gaussian (default), yukawa and theta are the same as above (SCB_FORCE_TYPE), with the same \(r_c\) and the same cutoff (COB_CUTOFF). Unlike the compartment force, the subcompartment Yukawa form correctly uses both beads.

In MultiMM

Key Default SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS False SCB_FORCE_TYPE gaussian SCB_EA1, SCB_EA2, SCB_EB1, SCB_EB2 1.0, 1.33, 1.66, 2.0 kJ/mol

Subcompartments need a CALDER-style .bed; a .bw track distinguishes only A from B. Both forces can be switched on together, in which case their energies add.

docs.title: Chromosome territories
docs.text:
In a genome-wide model every chromosome occupies its own region of the nucleus. A weak self-attraction inside each chromosome reproduces these territories.

With \(\chi_i\) the chromosome of bead \(i\), only pairs on the same chromosome interact, \(U_{ij}=\Delta E\,\delta(\chi_i,\chi_j)\,h(r_{ij})\) up to the sign convention of each form. Three shapes \(h\) are available (CHB_FORCE_TYPE), with \(k_C=\) CHB_KC and \(\Delta E=\) CHB_DE:

CHB_FORCE_TYPE Energy per pair (same chromosome) Character polynomial (default) \(\Delta E\,\bigl(k_Cr^4-r^3+r^2\bigr)\) Increases with \(r\) for \(k_C>9/32\approx0.28\) (the default 0.3 qualifies), so same-chromosome beads are always pulled together and the pull grows with separation (energy \(\sim r^4\)). Long-ranged, unbounded. gaussian \(-\Delta E\,e^{-k_Cr^2}\) A soft collapse kernel: attraction only within about \(1/\sqrt{2k_C}\approx1.3\) nm, and zero beyond. saturating \(-\dfrac{\Delta E}{1+k_Cr^2}\) Bounded, with a slow algebraic decay: it cannot over-compact a chromosome.

The default \(\Delta E=10^{-4}\) kJ/mol is tiny per pair, but the term acts on every same-chromosome pair, so its sum is large; for gaussian and saturating the same \(\Delta E\) is likely too weak, and you should raise it. This force has no cutoff. It is meaningful only with several chromosomes in one model (a warning is printed otherwise).

In MultiMM

Key Default CHB_USE_CHROMOSOMAL_BLOCKS False CHB_FORCE_TYPE polynomial CHB_KC (\(k_C\)), CHB_DE (\(\Delta E\)) 0.3, 0.0001

Why this force, and what does it model?

Chromosomes in a nucleus do not mix much: each occupies its own region, a territory. We model this with a weak attraction between beads of the same chromosome. It is weak on purpose, so that it only gathers the chromosome, and does not override the other forces.

docs.title: Choices in the data
docs.text:
Choice Effect .bed vs .bw A/B plus subcompartments, or A/B only COMPARTMENT_FLIP_PROB (default 0) Probability of flipping a bead's compartment identity A↔B; models uncertainty in the A/B call and gives variety in an ensemble COMPARTMENT_NOISE_STD (default 0) Standard deviation of Gaussian noise added to the compartment field before it is discretised again; moves compartment boundaries slightly

After a run, the 1D agreement with the input track and the 3D clustering of A and B beads are checked (metadata/compartment_validation.npy, metadata/compartment_aggregation.npy).

docs.title: Minimisation and molecular dynamics
docs.text:
The forces described in the previous pages define an energy \(E\) for every possible shape of the chromatin chain. This page explains the next step: how MultiMM finds good shapes, and how it can then make the chain move like a real, jiggling polymer. Everything here is controlled by a handful of SIM_* settings, and the defaults work for most runs.

In plain words

Think of \(E\) as a landscape of hills and valleys, where every position on the map is one possible folding of the chain. Minimisation is a hiker walking downhill to the bottom of the nearest valley: you get one comfortable shape. Molecular dynamics (MD) is the same hiker, but now warm and restless: the chain keeps jiggling around the valley floor, and the hiker takes a photo every now and then. You get a movie of plausible shapes.

docs.title: Why two steps?
docs.text:
Starting from the initial structure, the chain is compact and tidy, but it does not yet agree with your data. Minimisation fixes this quickly. It is cheap, deterministic, and for large systems (a whole chromosome or genome) it is often all you need.

A real chromosome, however, is never frozen in a single shape. Thermal motion makes it fluctuate constantly, and the cells in a sample each have a slightly different structure. MD mimics this. It is most useful for small and medium systems (a gene, a region) where you want

  • an ensemble of structures rather than one,
  • a measure of how flexible each part is (the RMSF, see below),
  • a check that the structure is stable, not just a lucky point of the landscape.

docs.title: Minimisation
docs.text:
MultiMM calls OpenMM's minimizeEnergy, which uses the L-BFGS method: at every step it moves all beads a little in the direction that lowers \(E\) the fastest, and it uses the memory of earlier steps to choose smart step sizes. It stops when the largest force on any bead is below a tolerance (10 kJ/mol/nm, the OpenMM default). The result is written to model/MultiMM_minimized.cif.

Minimisation always finishes in a local minimum, the nearest valley, which is why a good starting structure matters.

docs.title: What is integration?
docs.text:
To make the chain move we need Newton's law: force = mass × acceleration. For bead \(i\) with position \(\mathbf{r}_i\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}_i\),

\[ m\,\frac{d\mathbf{v}_i}{dt}=\mathbf{F}_i=-\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_i}E, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{r}_i}{dt}=\mathbf{v}_i . \]

In words: the energy tells us the force (a bead is pushed in the direction in which \(E\) decreases), the force changes the velocity, and the velocity changes the position. For more than two beads there is no formula for the answer, so the computer advances time in many tiny steps of length \(\Delta t\) (the time step). Integration means repeating this update step after step, and an integrator is the recipe for one update.

A recipe has to be good in two ways. It must be accurate, so that errors do not pile up, and it must be stable, so that the energy does not slowly drift. The simplest recipe (move along the current velocity, then update the velocity, called Euler) is neither, which is why MD programs use better ones such as the Verlet scheme:

\[ \mathbf{v}\leftarrow\mathbf{v}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2m}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}),\qquad \mathbf{r}\leftarrow\mathbf{r}+\Delta t\,\mathbf{v},\qquad \mathbf{v}\leftarrow\mathbf{v}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2m}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_\text{new}) . \]

First kick the velocity with the current force, then let the bead drift, then kick again with the new force. (OpenMM uses the equivalent leap-frog arrangement, which gives the same trajectory.) The Verlet scheme conserves energy very well, but it has no temperature control: it keeps whatever energy the system started with.

docs.title: The time step
docs.text:
The time step must be small compared with the fastest motion in the system, which here is the vibration of the stiff bonds. A step that is too large makes the energy explode (you will see NaN in the log). MultiMM uses 1 femtosecond (SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP), which is very safe. Each bead has the mass of 10 kb of chromatin (16 428 atomic mass units).

Time is relative

The lengths of the model are not physical nanometres (Units and scales), so the simulated time is not real time either. Use MD to compare relative fluctuations and to produce an ensemble, not to measure absolute speeds.

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text: Real chromatin sits in a bath at about 310 K, which keeps it jiggling. The integrators below that have a thermostat (Langevin, Brownian) imitate this: they add a little friction and random kicks, and the balance between the two keeps the average kinetic energy at \(\tfrac32k_BT\) per bead. The temperature is set by SIM_TEMPERATURE (default 310 K); it never needs to be changed unless you want to explore other conditions. Remember that \(k_BT\approx2.58\) kJ/mol at 310 K is the yardstick for how strong an interaction is.

docs.title: The integrators
docs.text:
SIM_INTEGRATOR_TYPE chooses the recipe. The default is langevin.

SIM_INTEGRATOR_TYPE Thermostat Settings it uses Use it for langevin (default) yes SIM_TEMPERATURE, SIM_FRICTION_COEFF, SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP almost everything brownian yes (overdamped) SIM_TEMPERATURE, SIM_FRICTION_COEFF, SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP slow, viscous motion; no inertia verlet no SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP tests; checking energy conservation variable_langevin yes SIM_TEMPERATURE, SIM_FRICTION_COEFF, SIM_ERROR_TOLERANCE automatic time step with a thermostat variable_verlet no SIM_ERROR_TOLERANCE automatic time step, no thermostat amd no SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP, SIM_AMD_ALPHA, SIM_AMD_E exploring beyond the nearest valley

docs.title: Langevin (default)
docs.text:
The Langevin integrator adds two ingredients to Newton's law. A friction \(-\gamma m\mathbf{v}\) slows the beads down, as if they moved through a thick liquid, and a random force kicks them, as if molecules of the liquid were hitting them:

\[ m\,\dot{\mathbf{v}}=-\nabla E-\gamma m\,\mathbf{v}+\sqrt{2\gamma m k_BT}\;\boldsymbol{\xi}(t), \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\) is random noise with zero average. Friction removes energy, the noise puts it back, and the balance is exactly the temperature \(T\) (the fluctuation-dissipation relation: the stronger the friction, the stronger the kicks needed).

  • SIM_FRICTION_COEFF is \(\gamma\), in 1/ps (default 0.5). Its inverse \(1/\gamma=2\) ps is the time it takes a bead to forget its velocity. A small \(\gamma\) gives inertial, quickly moving beads with a weak thermostat; a large \(\gamma\) gives slow, sticky motion. The static result (the average structure) does not depend on \(\gamma\), only the speed of exploring does.
  • SIM_TEMPERATURE is \(T\).
  • SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP is \(\Delta t\).

docs.title: Brownian
docs.text:
When friction is so large that velocities die out immediately, inertia does not matter and the beads simply diffuse while being pushed by the force. This is the overdamped limit, and is what the Brownian integrator computes:

\[ \mathbf{r}\leftarrow\mathbf{r}+\frac{\Delta t}{\gamma m}\,\mathbf{F}+\sqrt{\frac{2k_BT\,\Delta t}{\gamma m}}\;\boldsymbol{\xi}. \]

The first term is a drift along the force, the second a random walk. Chromatin lives in a very viscous nucleus, so this is often a realistic picture. It uses the same settings as Langevin, but velocities play no role.

docs.title: Verlet
docs.text: The plain Verlet scheme above, with no thermostat. It conserves the total energy: the temperature is whatever the starting velocities (and the energy released by the structure relaxing) give, and it can drift. It uses only SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP. Choose it for tests and to check that the time step is small enough (the total energy in the plots should stay flat).

docs.title: Variable-step integrators
docs.text: variable_verlet and variable_langevin choose the time step by themselves. After every step they estimate the integration error by comparing the result with a simpler method, and they shrink or grow \(\Delta t\) to keep that error below SIM_ERROR_TOLERANCE (default 0.01). They have no fixed time step, so SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP is ignored, and the simulated time per MD step varies. They are useful when you are unsure which step is safe. A smaller tolerance means a more careful, slower run.

docs.title: Accelerated MD (amd)
docs.text:
Chromatin can sit in a valley for a very long time because the hills around it are high. Accelerated MD lifts the valley floors, so the chain crosses the hills more easily. Whenever the energy \(V\) is below a threshold \(E_\text{thr}\), the force is rescaled as if the energy were

\[ V^*=V+\frac{(E_\text{thr}-V)^2}{\alpha+E_\text{thr}-V}, \]

and unchanged otherwise (OpenMM, following Hamelberg et al. 2007).

  • SIM_AMD_E is the threshold \(E_\text{thr}\) in kJ/mol (default 1000). Valleys deeper than this are lifted.
  • SIM_AMD_ALPHA is \(\alpha\) in kJ/mol (default 100). A small \(\alpha\) flattens the landscape more strongly (a stronger boost); a large \(\alpha\) is gentler.

The numbers must be adapted to the size of your system, because the total energy grows with the number of beads. AMD has no thermostat, and the structures it samples come from a modified landscape, so use it for exploration, not for reading off thermodynamic averages.

Which one should I use?

Keep langevin unless you have a reason. Use brownian if you want purely diffusive motion, verlet only for tests, and amd only to explore further than the nearest valley. If a run produces NaN, reduce SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP or try a variable_* integrator.

docs.title: How long, and what is saved
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning SIM_RUN_MD False run MD after the minimisation (presets such as GENE switch it on) SIM_N_STEPS 10 000 total number of time steps SIM_SAMPLING_STEP 100 save a frame every this many steps (so 100 frames by default) TRJ_FRAMES none if set, exactly this many frames are saved (it overrides SIM_SAMPLING_STEP) SIM_SET_INITIAL_VELOCITIES True draw the starting velocities from the temperature, so that the system starts at the right \(T\)

The frames are written to md_frames/, together with a trajectory file metadata/MultiMM_annealing.dcd, and the last structure is model/MultiMM_afterMD.cif. With SAVE_PLOTS on, MultiMM also reports how the run went:

  • the energy of every force term over time (plots/energy_components.png), which shows which force is doing the work,
  • the potential, kinetic and total energy and the temperature, computed from the kinetic energy (it should hover around SIM_TEMPERATURE),
  • the RMSD from the minimised structure (how far the chain wanders),
  • the RMSF of every bead (how flexible each part is), and the distribution of velocities, which should look like a bell curve.

How do I know that the run is long enough?

Look at the energy components and the RMSD: when they stop drifting and just fluctuate around a level, the structure has relaxed. If they are still going up or down at the end, increase SIM_N_STEPS.

docs.title: Hi-C force
docs.text:
A Hi-C map counts how often each pair of genomic bins was found in contact. MultiMM turns this map into distance restraints between beads, so that the 3D structure reproduces the map. The idea is Boltzmann inversion: if contact frequency decreases with distance, a measured frequency can be converted back into a distance.

In plain words

A Hi-C map tells us which pairs of genome regions hug often. Pairs that hug often must be close; pairs that never hug are probably far. For every pair that hugs we tie a rubber band between the two beads, with a length that is shorter for a stronger hug. The folded structure is the one in which most rubber bands are relaxed.

docs.title: Step 1: preparing the matrix
docs.text:
The raw map is cleaned and brought to the bead resolution before it is used. Each step is applied in this order:

  1. Load and normalise (HIC_NORMALIZATION): KR (default), VC, VC_SQRT or NONE correct experimental biases. Short runs of empty bins (up to HIC_MAX_GAP bins in a row) are filled by interpolation.
  2. Clean: symmetrise, remove NaN, negative values and the diagonal.
  3. Resize to exactly \(N\) beads by weighted averaging (or interpolation if the map is coarser than the model).
  4. Optional \(O/E\) (HIC_FORCE_OE): contacts naturally decay with genomic distance, which dominates the map. The observed/expected ratio divides this decay out, and the force uses only the enrichment above background, \(\max(O/E-1,\,0)\), so that only pairs that touch more than expected attract.
  5. Denoise: a \(3\times3\) median filter removes isolated pixels, values above the 99th percentile are capped, and a light Gaussian smoothing (\(\sigma=1.5\) beads) is applied.
  6. Rescale so that the largest entry is 1. The result \(c_{ij}\in[0,1]\) is the contact strength of beads \(i,j\).

docs.title: Step 2: Boltzmann inversion, from contact strength to distance
docs.text:
This is the key idea of the force, so it is worth spelling out.

Boltzmann distribution. For a system in equilibrium at temperature \(T\), the probability of finding two beads at distance \(r\) is related to their interaction energy \(U(r)\) by

\[ P(r)\;\propto\;e^{-U(r)/k_BT}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad U(r)=-k_BT\,\ln P(r). \]

Low energy means high probability: pairs prefer distances where \(U\) is small. The energy defined this way is called the potential of mean force (it includes the effect of all other beads, not only the pair itself).

Inversion. A Hi-C map measures how often two loci touch, which is proportional to \(P(r)\) at a small distance. So the experiment gives us the left-hand side of the relation above, and we need the right-hand side: an energy that would produce these frequencies. Going from measured probabilities back to an energy (or to a preferred distance) is called Boltzmann inversion. In MultiMM it is done in two small steps:

  1. Choose a model for how the contact probability falls with distance, \(P(r)\) (the kernel, three options below). It is scaled so that \(P=1\) at the smallest distance \(r_\text{min}\) (the bead size) and decreases for larger \(r\).
  2. For each pair, take its contact strength \(c_{ij}\in[0,1]\) as the probability and solve \(P(r_t)=c_{ij}\) for the distance \(r_t\). Strong contact gives a short \(r_t\), weak contact a long one.

Example with the default kernel \(P(r)=e^{-(r-r_\text{min})/\lambda}\): the corresponding energy \(-k_BT\ln P=k_BT\,(r-r_\text{min})/\lambda\) grows linearly with distance, and the inversion gives \(r_t=r_\text{min}-\lambda\ln c_{ij}\). A pair with \(c=1\) wants \(r_\text{min}\), a pair with \(c=0.1\) wants about \(2.3\lambda\) farther away.

The distance cannot exceed a maximum \(r_c\), the contact radius (see below), beyond which a pair is not considered "in contact". The steepness is set by \(\alpha\) (HIC_BOLTZMANN_ALPHA, 4 by default, close to the typical Hi-C decay exponent). The three kernels differ only in the assumed shape of \(P(r)\):

HIC_BOLTZMANN_KERNEL \(P(r)\) Target distance \(r_t(c)\) Character exponential (default) \(e^{-(r-r_\text{min})/\lambda}\), \(\lambda=r_c/\alpha\) \(r_\text{min}-\lambda\ln c\) The classic Boltzmann distribution: \(P\propto e^{-U/k_BT}\) with an energy that grows linearly with distance. Moderate decay. power_law \((r_\text{min}/r)^{\alpha}\) \(r_\text{min}\,c^{-1/\alpha}\) Heavy-tailed, mimics the measured \(c\sim r^{-\alpha}\) decay. Weak contacts are mapped to very long distances (clipped at \(r_c\)). sigmoid \(\dfrac{1}{1+e^{k(r-r_0)}}\), \(r_0=\tfrac{r_\text{min}+r_c}{2},\ k=\tfrac{\alpha}{r_c}\) \(r_0-\tfrac1k\ln\dfrac{c}{1-c}\) A smooth switch between "in contact" and "not in contact" around the midpoint \(r_0\); distances are compressed to the middle of \([r_\text{min},r_c]\).

The target is always clipped to \([r_\text{min},\,r_c]\). Plotted the other way round, the kernels differ in how they treat weak contacts:

docs.title: Step 3: the restraint energy
docs.text:
Each contacted pair becomes a spring between the two beads, centred on the target distance \(r_t\) from the inversion and weighted by the contact strength \(c_{ij}\):

\[ U_{ij}(r)=\tfrac12\,k\,c_{ij}\,(r-r_t)^2 , \]

where \(k\) is the global stiffness (HIC_K_SCALE, 40 kJ/mol by default). Think of it as a rubber band that wants the two beads at distance \(r_t\):

  • Force. The force is \(-\partial U/\partial r=-k\,c_{ij}\,(r-r_t)\). Beads farther apart than \(r_t\) are pulled together, and beads closer than \(r_t\) are pushed apart. It vanishes at \(r_t\) and grows linearly, so there are no jumps.
  • Strength \(c_{ij}\) as stiffness. A strong contact is a stiff band and a weak contact a soft one. Noisy low-count pixels therefore hardly constrain the structure, while well-measured contacts dominate.
  • Global strength \(k\). It has to beat thermal motion (\(k_BT\approx2.6\) kJ/mol) to be felt, but a bead has many Hi-C partners whose pulls add up, so very large values freeze the dynamics. Values of 20 to 160 are recommended.
  • A compromise. A bead cannot be at its target distance from all partners at once. The structure settles where the total energy \(\sum_{i<j}U_{ij}\) is lowest, a weighted least-squares fit of all target distances: strong, consistent contacts are satisfied and weak or inconsistent ones are partly violated.

Weak contacts only push, never pull. A weak background contact is mapped by the kernel to the maximum distance \(r_c\), but it only says "not enriched", not "exactly \(r_c\) apart". If such pairs were pulled to \(r_c\), the huge number of weak pairs would all demand the same distance, and in 3D the only way to satisfy this is to spread the beads over a spherical shell. So for these pairs the spring acts only when the beads are closer than \(r_c\) (it pushes them apart) and is switched off beyond. Pairs with real evidence (\(r_t<r_c\)) keep the full two-sided spring above. This is decided automatically from the data and is not a parameter.

docs.title: The contact radius \(r_c\)
docs.text:
\(r_c\) has to be on the scale of the actual structure. MultiMM chooses it in this order:

  1. If HIC_RC is set, it is used as is.
  2. Else, if HIC_AUTO_SCALE is True (default), \(r_c\) is the median pairwise distance of the initial structure, so most contacted pairs start within reach of the force.
  3. Else (or if the calibration fails), the nucleus-scale fallback \(r_c=R_2/3\) is used (Units and scales).

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
• Noise (HIC_NOISE_INTENSITY, default 0): at every saved MD frame each \(c_{ij}\) is redrawn as a Gaussian around its original value (clipped to \([0,1]\)), with this standard deviation, so the sampling explores nearby configurations rather than one attractor. Targets \(r_t\) stay fixed.
  • Hi-C-derived compartments (HIC_BLOCK_COPOLYMER, default False): the Boltzmann force reproduces diagonal decay and domains well, but tends to miss the plaid compartment pattern. With this option the compartments are taken from the first principal component (PC1) of the Hi-C map, signed so that dense regions are B and sparse regions are A, and fed into the compartment force, so no .bed file is needed. It works only with HIC_USE_FORCE=True and no compartment file, is switched off automatically for regions shorter than HIC_BLOCK_COPOLYMER_MIN_BP (5 Mb), and raises an error if COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS or SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS is also on.
  • Validation: after the run, the structure's contact map is compared with the input map using several metrics, for example correlation of contacts, of the \(P(s)\) decay and of the insulation score (window HIC_INSULATION_WINDOW beads, default 10), against a random-walk baseline (metadata/hic_validation.npy).

In MultiMM

docs.title: Initial structure
docs.text:
Energy minimisation is a local search: it slides downhill from wherever it starts. For a chain of tens of thousands of beads, a random starting coil is badly knotted and the optimiser gets trapped in poor minima. MultiMM therefore starts from a designed conformation that is already compact and ordered. The default is a Hilbert curve.

In plain words

Finding the best folding is easier if you start from a tidy, compact fold than from a tangled mess. The Hilbert curve is such a tidy fold: a path that winds through a cube without ever crossing itself.

docs.title: Why do we need a starting structure at all?
docs.text:
The computer cannot find the answer in one step. It has to start from a guess and improve it, like a hiker who is dropped somewhere in the mountains and walks downhill to find a valley. The energy \(E\) of the chain is a landscape over all the bead positions, with many valleys, most of them not very deep. The valley we end up in depends on where we started.

If the starting guess is a tangled random coil, the chain is full of knots that cannot be undone, because beads cannot pass through each other, and the hiker gets stuck in a poor valley. If the guess is already neat and compact, the hiker only needs a small walk to reach a good one. This is also faster, which matters for chains of tens of thousands of beads. So the starting structure is not the answer; it is a good place to start looking.

docs.title: The Hilbert curve
docs.text:
A Hilbert curve is a continuous path that visits every point of a cubic lattice exactly once. In three dimensions with order \(p\), the lattice has \(2^p\times2^p\times2^p\) points, and the curve is a map

\[ H:\{0,1,\dots,2^{3p}-1\}\;\longrightarrow\;\{0,\dots,2^p-1\}^3 . \]

Two properties make it ideal as a chromatin starting point:

  1. Chain connectivity. Consecutive points are always lattice neighbours, \(\lVert H(d+1)-H(d)\rVert_1 = 1\), so the chain never has to stretch to stay connected.
  2. Locality and nesting. The first \(8^k\) points fill a cube of side \(2^k\) completely, and points that are close along the curve stay close in space. A stretch of consecutive beads (a chromosome) therefore occupies a compact, contiguous region. This is exactly the picture of chromosome territories, and it is also why the curve resembles the fractal globule, a knot-free compact polymer state often used to describe chromatin.

In MultiMM

MultiMM takes the first \(N\) points of a 3D Hilbert curve of order \(p=8\) (a \(256^3\) lattice) and uses them as bead positions. The lattice spacing is one unit, which is written to the structure file as 1 Å \(=0.1\) nm, the same as the bond length \(b_0\) (see Units and scales). The chain therefore starts with bonds that are already at their rest length.

The bounding cube of the curve has volume about \(N b_0^3\), whereas the nuclear sphere has volume \(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}R_2^3\approx4.2\,N b_0^3\). The initial structure thus fills roughly a quarter of the container: compact, but with room to expand and rearrange.

In a genome-wide run all chromosomes are concatenated into one chain, with one block of beads per chromosome. Bonds and angles are not applied across chromosome boundaries, so chromosomes remain separate polymers although they share one Hilbert curve. With SHUFFLE_CHROMS = True the order of chromosomes along the chain is randomised before the curve is laid down (seeded by SHUFFLING_SEED), which changes which chromosomes start as neighbours. This is useful for ensembles, because the final arrangement of territories should not depend on an arbitrary order.

docs.title: Alternative starting structures
docs.text:
All other options place beads with a nominal step of one unit (\(=b_0\)). They are mostly useful for testing, for ensembles that should forget the Hilbert order, or for small regions where compaction is not an issue.

docs.title: Nuclear organisation and lamina
docs.text:
At genome scale, chromatin is not free: it sits inside the nucleus, and its position is not random. Heterochromatin (B) is enriched at the nuclear lamina, the protein mesh lining the nuclear envelope, while small, gene-rich chromosomes tend to sit toward the interior near the nucleolus. MultiMM encodes this with three optional radial forces. All of them act on the distance \(r\) of a bead from the centre of mass of the structure.

In plain words

The nucleus is a ball with a wall (the lamina) and, in the middle, a dense region (the nucleolus). Inactive chromatin likes to cling to the walls, while small chromosomes like to sit toward the centre. The forces on this page just express these preferences.

The sketch is a schematic. One chromosome (bead chain) is shown: its B segments (purple) stay near the lamina and its A segments (gold) farther inside. In the model the sizes follow from the number of beads (see Units and scales): \(R_2=b_0N^{1/3}\) is the nuclear radius and \(R_1=0.2^{1/3}R_2\approx0.58R_2\) is the radius of the inner region, which corresponds to 20% of the nuclear volume and plays the role of the nucleolus.

docs.title: Spherical container
docs.text:
Beads are confined to the shell \(R_1<r<R_2\) by a soft wall on both sides:

\[ U_\text{container}(r)=C\,\bigl[\max(0,\,r-R_2)^2+\max(0,\,R_1-r)^2\bigr], \]

with \(C=\) SC_SCALE. Inside the shell the energy is zero; outside it grows quadratically, so the wall is a harmonic one, and strong (\(C=1000\) by default).

In MultiMM

Key Default SC_USE_SPHERICAL_CONTAINER False (the genome-wide preset GW switches it on) SC_SCALE (\(C\)) 1000.0

SC_RADIUS1 and SC_RADIUS2 exist in the configuration but are not used: the radii always follow from \(N\).

Why this force, and what does it model?

The nucleus has a boundary, and chromatin cannot leave it. A soft wall is the simplest way to say this: the energy is zero inside and rises quickly outside, so beads can move freely in the nucleus but are pushed back at its edge. The inner wall plays the role of the nucleolus, which chromatin avoids.

docs.title: B-lamina interaction
docs.text:
Only B beads (\(s_i=-1\) or \(-2\)) feel this force (A beads and unassigned beads have zero energy). It pulls B chromatin toward the lamina. Four radial profiles are available (BLAMINA_FORCE_TYPE); \(B=\) IBL_SCALE, \(r_0=\tfrac12(R_1+R_2)\) is the middle of the shell.

BLAMINA_FORCE_TYPE Energy of a B bead Character sin (default) \(B\left[\sin^8\!\left(\pi\frac{\bar r-R_1}{R_2-R_1}\right)-1\right]\), \(\bar r=\min(\max(r,R_1),R_2)\) Minimum \(-B\) at both walls and maximum \(0\) in the middle of the shell. The high power makes the wells narrow. Outside the shell \(r\) is clamped, so the energy stays at \(-B\) (no periodic bumps). gaussian_shell \(-B\left[e^{-\frac{(r-R_1)^2}{2\sigma^2}}+e^{-\frac{(r-R_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\right]\), \(\sigma=0.1(R_2-R_1)\) Two Gaussian wells of depth \(B\) at the walls, vanishing away from them. harmonic_shell $-B\,\left[\dfrac{\min( r-r_0 logistic_shell \(-B\left[\operatorname{sech}^2\!\frac{r-R_1}{2\lambda}+\operatorname{sech}^2\!\frac{r-R_2}{2\lambda}\right]\), \(\lambda=0.1(R_2-R_1)\) Two smooth (logistic-derivative) wells of depth \(B\) at the walls with soft tails.

All four share the same logic: the maximum is in the middle of the shell and the minima (\(-B\)) sit at the radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2\). They differ only in how wide and how sharp the wells are. Here \(\operatorname{sech}x=1/\cosh x\).

In MultiMM

Key Default IBL_USE_B_LAMINA_INTERACTION False (requires COMPARTMENT_PATH; switched on by the GW preset when a compartment file is given) BLAMINA_FORCE_TYPE sin IBL_SCALE (\(B\)) 400.0 kJ/mol

Why this force, and what does it model?

Heterochromatin is attached to the lamina through proteins, so B beads feel a well near the wall. The different forms only change how wide and how sharp this well is.

docs.title: Central force (chromosome-size positioning)
docs.text:
Small chromosomes are found closer to the interior, large ones toward the periphery. The central force reproduces this with a bias that depends on chromosome size. Each bead carries a weight \(\chi_i\in[0,1]\) given by its chromosome length, rescaled so that the shortest chromosome has \(\chi=1\) and the longest \(\chi=0\), i.e. the force acts mostly on small chromosomes. With \(G=\) CF_STRENGTH and \(\sigma\), \(\lambda\) derived from \(R_1\):

CENTRAL_FORCE_TYPE Energy of bead \(i\) Character harmonic (default) \(G\chi_i\,(r-R_1)^2\) A parabola whose minimum (energy \(0\)) sits exactly at \(R_1\); all three forms have their minimum at \(R_1\): small chromosomes are pulled toward the nucleolus surface from both sides, and pay a penalty \(G\chi_i(r-R_1)^2\) for straying. gaussian \(-G\chi_i\,e^{-(r-R_1)^2/(2\sigma^2)},\ \sigma=0.3R_1\) A Gaussian well with its minimum \(-G\chi_i\) at \(R_1\): the energy slopes down gently and flattens smoothly into the minimum, so small chromosomes are drawn to the nucleolus surface. logistic \(-G\chi_i\,\operatorname{sech}^2\!\big((r-R_1)/\lambda\big),\ \lambda=0.25R_1\) A bell-shaped well (hyperbolic secant squared) with its minimum \(-G\chi_i\) at \(R_1\). It has longer tails than the Gaussian, so the pull is felt from further away and increases smoothly toward \(R_1\).

In MultiMM

Key Default CF_USE_CENTRAL_FORCE False CENTRAL_FORCE_TYPE harmonic CF_STRENGTH (\(G\)) 20.0 kJ/mol

The chromosome weights \(\chi_i\) come from the chromosome lengths of the model, so this force needs a multi-chromosome (genome-wide) run to be meaningful.

Why this force, and what does it model?

Gene-poor, large chromosomes tend to be near the periphery and small, gene-rich ones in the interior, a trend seen in many cell types. We express it with a bias that grows as the chromosome gets smaller: a weak pull towards the centre, so it nudges the arrangement without forcing it.

Typical genome-wide setup

Container on, B-lamina on (with a compartment file), central force off. This is what the GW preset configures; see Advanced options.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
A chromatin loop is a pair of genomic positions, usually bound by CTCF and cohesin, that touch frequently although they are far apart along the chromosome. Loops are the main source of short- and medium-range structure in MultiMM: they create loops, nested loops and, through their clustering, TAD-like domains.

In plain words

A loop is like tying two far-apart points of a long rope together with a short elastic band. The rest of the rope bulges out in between, and that bulge is the loop.

MultiMM models each loop as a bond between two distant beads.

docs.title: From loop calls to a loop list
docs.text:
The input is a .bedpe file in which every row lists the two anchors of a loop and a strength (a contact count, a peak score, or 1 for single-cell data); see Input data. The rows are turned into triples \((m_\ell,\,n_\ell,\,d_\ell)\): the two anchor beads of loop \(\ell\) and its target distance.

  1. Select the loops that lie entirely inside the modelled region. In a genome-wide run the chromosomes are placed one after another on a single axis.
  2. Take anchor midpoints. Anchors are intervals but a bead is a point, so each anchor is reduced to its midpoint.
  3. Rescale to beads. A genomic coordinate becomes a bead index by dividing by the resolution (Units and scales).
  4. Aggregate. Loops that land on the same pair of beads are merged and their strengths averaged into one value \(c_\ell\). Loops whose anchors are closer than three beads (\(n_\ell\le m_\ell+2\)) are dropped: the backbone already holds such beads together.
  5. Convert strength to distance (below).

docs.title: From strength to distance
docs.text:
A strong loop means frequent contact, so a short distance. Hi-C contact frequency falls with distance roughly as a power law, which can be inverted: the stronger the loop, the shorter the distance. MultiMM uses

\[ d_\ell \;=\; 0.1 + 0.1\,\tilde c_\ell\ \text{nm},\qquad \tilde c_\ell=\operatorname{minmax}\!\left(c_\ell^{-2/3}\right)\in[0,1], \]

where \(\operatorname{minmax}\) rescales the values over all loops to \([0,1]\). The strongest loop gets 0.1 nm and the weakest 0.2 nm: strength only orders the distances inside a narrow range, and every loop pulls its anchors close together.

Loops of equal strength

If all loops have the same strength (typical for single-cell data where strength is 1) the rescaling is undefined and the code sets every \(d_\ell=1\) nm, which is not a tight loop. For such data set LE_FIXED_DISTANCES = True: every loop then uses LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 instead.

docs.title: The loop force
docs.text:
Each loop is a bond with rest length \(r_0=d_\ell\) (or LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 if LE_FIXED_DISTANCES = True) and stiffness \(k\) (LE_HARMONIC_BOND_K). Write \(x=r_{m_\ell n_\ell}-r_0\) for the deviation from the target. Three shapes are available, selected with LE_LOOP_FORCE_TYPE:

LE_LOOP_FORCE_TYPE Energy per loop Behaviour harmonic (default) \(\dfrac{k}{2}\,x^2\) Classic spring. The restoring force grows without limit as the loop is stretched, so every loop is enforced strictly. Best when you trust the loop calls. fene_soft \(\dfrac{k\,x^2}{1+\alpha x^2},\ \alpha=\dfrac1{r_0^2}\) Quadratic for small \(x\) (note: \(k x^2\), twice the harmonic stiffness) but saturates at \(k\,r_0^2\) (300 kJ/mol for the defaults). A badly violated loop stops pulling harder. gaussian_tether \(k\left(1-e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}\right),\ \sigma=\dfrac{r_0}{2}\) A smooth well that is zero at the target and flat at \(k\) far away (30 000 kJ/mol for the defaults, but note that this plateau is an energy, while for the other two \(k\) is a spring constant). The force vanishes for very stretched loops, and near the target the curvature is \(4k/r_0^2\), which is much stiffer than the others.

The two bounded forms are meant for noisy or partly inconsistent loop sets (loops from different cells, false positives): with a harmonic bond one wrong loop can distort the structure, while a bounded bond limits the damage. Because \(k\) means different things in the three forms, re-tune LE_HARMONIC_BOND_K when you switch the form.

Loops here are static restraints

The prefix LE comes from loop extrusion, the mechanism that forms loops in cells, but MultiMM does not simulate cohesin moving along DNA. It places one fixed bond for every observed loop, and the structure is the best arrangement consistent with all of them.

docs.title: Why do loops make TADs?
docs.text:
A bond between two beads pins a loop in the chain. Many loops with anchors in the same neighbourhood hold a stretch of chromatin in a compact cluster while beads outside are free to move away. After minimisation this is a domain with many internal contacts and a clear boundary, which is the TAD signal in a Hi-C map. Domain boundaries in a MultiMM structure therefore come from where the loop anchors lie.

Why this force, and what does it model?

Loops are made by proteins (cohesin and CTCF) that hold two sites together. In the model we do not simulate the proteins; we only say the sites are held at a short distance, with a spring. Each loop is a measured fact, so the spring is the minimal way to put that fact into the structure. The softer forms (fene_soft, gaussian_tether) exist because a pure spring can pull very hard if a loop is not consistent with the rest of the data, and a bounded force is gentler.

docs.text:
Choice Effect Assay (HiCCUPS, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, CTCF/cohesin) Decides which loops exist. ChIA-PET and HiChIP loops are sparse and strong; Hi-C loop calls are denser. Strength column Only the ranking of strengths matters (above). LE_FIXED_DISTANCES True: all loops use LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0. False (default): distance from strength. DOWNSAMPLING_PROB Keeps a random fraction of the loops, so each ensemble member uses a different subset.

In MultiMM
