The anchors and distances actually used are saved as metadata/ms.npy, ns.npy and ds.npy, and a loop-validation summary as metadata/loop_validation.npy.

docs.title: Units and scales
docs.text:
Every force in MultiMM needs a length or an energy to be meaningful ("how far apart are bonded beads?", "how big is the nucleus?", "how strong is an attraction compared with thermal motion?"). Rather than asking you to choose all of these independently, MultiMM derives almost every scale from one microscopic length and the number of beads. This page lists those definitions in one place.

In plain words

It is like the scale on a map: we choose one length (the distance between neighbouring beads) and then measure every other size, such as the radius of the nucleus, in terms of it. You only choose how many beads you want; MultiMM works out the rest.

docs.title: One length unit: the bond length
docs.text:
The basic length is the bond length \(b_0\) (POL_HARMONIC_BOND_R0, default \(0.1\) nm). It is the preferred distance between consecutive beads, and the other geometric quantities are written in terms of it.

Lengths are model units

A bead represents a stretch of chromatin of several kilobases, whose true physical size is tens of nanometres, but \(b_0\) is only \(0.1\) nm. The "nm" in the configuration is a label for the length unit of the simulation, chosen so that the numbers behave well in OpenMM. Compare structures with each other, and with Hi-C, in relative terms. To compare with microscopy, rescale lengths by the physical size of one bead (or by the radius of your nucleus).

docs.title: Genomic resolution
docs.text:
The number of beads \(N\) (N_BEADS) sets the genomic length represented by one bead:

\[ \text{resolution}=\frac{\text{modelled genomic length}}{N}\ \text{bp per bead}. \]

For a region the length is LOC_END - LOC_START; for a whole chromosome it is its length; for the whole genome it is the sum of the chromosome lengths. Examples: a 13 Mb region with \(N=5000\) gives about 2.6 kb per bead; the autosomes with \(N=50\,000\) give about 60 kb per bead.

All input data are mapped onto this grid. A genomic coordinate \(x\) becomes the bead index \(\lfloor (x-x_\text{start})/\text{resolution}\rfloor\). A loop anchor, a compartment interval and a Hi-C bin are all converted this way.

docs.title: The geometric scales
docs.text:
From \(b_0\) and \(N\) MultiMM computes the size of the nucleus. The idea is a dense globule of constant density: a volume that grows in proportion to the number of beads, so the radius grows as \(N^{1/3}\).

Quantity Definition Meaning Nuclear radius \(R_2\) \(R_2=b_0\,N^{1/3}\) Outer wall of the nucleus (nuclear envelope, lamina) Inner radius \(R_1\) \(R_1=R_2\,f^{1/3}\) with \(f=0.2\) Surface of an excluded central sphere (the nucleolus) that holds 20% of the volume Compartment range \(r_c\) \(r_c=R_2/3\) Width of the compartment and subcompartment attraction Contact cutoff \(r_\text{cut}\) \(r_\text{cut}=5\,b_0\) Hard cutoff beyond which compartment forces are ignored Excluded-volume size \(\sigma\) LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 (default 0.1) Length scale of bead repulsion Loop distance \(d\) between \(0.1\) and \(0.2\) Rest length of a loop bond (see Loops) Hi-C contact radius \(r_\text{c}^\text{Hi-C}\) median pairwise distance of the initial structure, or HIC_RC Largest target distance of the Hi-C force Hi-C minimum distance \(r_\text{min}\) LE_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 Smallest target distance of the Hi-C force

The nucleus is centred on the centroid of the initial structure, which is the origin of the radial coordinate \(r\) in all radial forces.

In MultiMM

Only \(b_0\) and \(N\) are free. The nucleolus fraction \(f=0.2\) is fixed. \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) always follow from \(b_0\) and \(N\); the keys SC_RADIUS1 and SC_RADIUS2 exist but are not used.

A worked example, for the default \(b_0=0.1\) nm:

\(N\) \(R_2\) \(R_1\) \(r_c=R_2/3\) \(r_\text{cut}\) 1 000 1.00 0.58 0.33 0.5 5 000 1.71 1.00 0.57 0.5 50 000 3.68 2.15 1.23 0.5 200 000 5.85 3.42 1.95 0.5

Why the cutoff does not grow with \(N\)

\(R_2\) and \(r_c\) grow with the system, but the compartment cutoff stays at \(5\,b_0\). Compartment forces are meant to be local contact attractions: without a cutoff, OpenMM would sum every pair in the system, and the total attraction would then grow with \(N\) instead of with the local density, which makes large structures collapse. Inside the cutoff the Gaussian profile is shallow, so the force acts almost like a contact attraction. See Compartments.

docs.title: Energy and temperature
docs.text:
Energies are in kJ/mol and the temperature is 310 K (SIM_TEMPERATURE). The thermal energy is

\[ k_BT = 0.008314\ \tfrac{\text{kJ}}{\text{mol K}}\times 310\ \text{K}\approx 2.58\ \text{kJ/mol}. \]

It helps to read force strengths in units of \(k_BT\):

Force Default In units of \(k_BT\) Bond stiffness \(k_b\) \(3\times10^{5}\) kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻² thermal bond stretch \(\sqrt{k_BT/k_b}\approx0.003\) nm, about 3% of \(b_0\): bonds are nearly rigid Angle stiffness \(k_\theta\) 100 kJ mol⁻¹ rad⁻² rms bending of about 0.23 rad per joint Excluded volume \(\varepsilon\) 100 kJ/mol repulsion of \(\approx3.4\,k_BT\) at \(r=b_0\), \(\approx39\,k_BT\) at \(r=b_0/2\) Compartment attraction \(E_A\), \(E_B\) 1 and 2 kJ/mol 0.39 and 0.78 \(k_BT\) per contact: weak, so compartments form collectively Hi-C stiffness 40 see Hi-C force

Individual attractions are much weaker than \(k_BT\) on purpose. A bead has many neighbours, so many weak contacts add up to a strong collective preference, which is the mechanism behind phase separation.

docs.title: Mass, time and friction
docs.text: Each bead carries the theoretical mass of 10 kb of chromatin, \(16\,427.889\) amu (set in the bundled force field file ff.xml). The integration step is SIM_INTEGRATOR_STEP (default 1 fs) and the Langevin friction is SIM_FRICTION_COEFF (default 0.5 ps⁻¹). Because lengths are in model units, simulated time should be read as an optimisation clock rather than as real time.

docs.title: Writing a config file
docs.text:
The config file is where you tell MultiMM what to do. It is just a text file with lines like N_BEADS = 1000, and you only write the settings you want to change. If you make a typo, MultiMM will stop and suggest the right name, so there is no harm in trying.

A config file is a plain text file in INI format: a list of KEY = value lines. You only need to write the keys you want to change; everything else keeps its default (see Arguments for all keys and defaults).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• One section. Put everything under a header such as [Main]. The name of the section does not matter.
  • Keys are the argument names in capitals, exactly as in Arguments. An unknown key stops the run and the error suggests the closest valid name, so typos are caught early.
  • Comments start with ; or #, either on their own line or after a value.
  • Booleans can be True/False, yes/no or 1/0.
  • Numbers are written plainly. Large integers may use underscores for readability, for example 160_000_000.
  • Quantities (a value with a unit) are written as a number, a space and a unit name: 0.1 nanometer, 310 kelvin, 1 femtosecond, 300000.0 kilojoules_per_mole/nanometer**2. A bare number is not accepted for these keys.
  • Empty or missing means "not used". An empty value for an optional path, for example HIC_PATH =, is the same as not setting it.
  • Paths can be absolute or relative to the folder where you run the command.
  • Chromosomes are written as chr1 or just 1.

docs.title: A first example: a region with loops and compartments
docs.text:
[Main]
; --- what to model ---
CHROM     = chr1
LOC_START = 160_000_000
LOC_END   = 173_000_000
N_BEADS   = 5000                 ; resolution is (LOC_END - LOC_START) / N_BEADS

; --- data ---
LOOPS_PATH       = data/loops.bedpe
COMPARTMENT_PATH = data/compartments.bed

; --- forces: loops on, compartment force on ---
LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND       = True
COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS = True

; --- output ---
OUT_PATH = results/chr1_region

docs.title: Driving the structure with a Hi-C map
docs.text:
Without loops the loop term must be switched off, and the Hi-C force switched on:

[Main]
CHROM     = chr1
LOC_START = 160_000_000
LOC_END   = 173_000_000
N_BEADS   = 5000

HIC_PATH      = data/map.hic
HIC_USE_FORCE = True
HIC_K_SCALE   = 40.0
HIC_BOLTZMANN_KERNEL = exponential

LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND = False     ; no loop file in this run
OUT_PATH = results/chr1_hic

docs.title: A genome-wide model
docs.text:
[Main]
MODELLING_LEVEL = GW             ; preset: 200000 beads, container on, MD off
LOOPS_PATH       = data/loops.bedpe
COMPARTMENT_PATH = data/subcompartments.bed
SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS = True
PLATFORM = CUDA
OUT_PATH = results/genome

Remember that a preset overwrites some parameters (Advanced options).

docs.title: Changing physical parameters
docs.text:
Backbone, force-field and simulation parameters have sensible defaults and mostly do not need to be set. When you do, remember the units and the model scales (Units and scales):

POL_HARMONIC_BOND_R0 = 0.1 nanometer
POL_HARMONIC_ANGLE_CONSTANT_K = 200.0 kilojoules_per_mole/radian**2
EV_FORCE_TYPE = gaussian_core
LE_LOOP_FORCE_TYPE = fene_soft
SIM_TEMPERATURE = 310 kelvin

docs.title: Dependencies between keys
docs.text:
Some switches only make sense together with an input file or with each other. In particular:

If you enable you also need LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND (on by default) LOOPS_PATH COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS, SCB_USE_SUBCOMPARTMENT_BLOCKS COMPARTMENT_PATH IBL_USE_B_LAMINA_INTERACTION COMPARTMENT_PATH HIC_USE_FORCE HIC_PATH HIC_BLOCK_COPOLYMER HIC_USE_FORCE and no compartment force MODELLING_LEVEL = GENE GENE_NAME or GENE_ID CHROM LOC_START and LOC_END (or the CHROM preset)

Keep a record

Every run saves the complete, resolved configuration (defaults included) as metadata/config_auto.ini, so any result can be reproduced by passing that file to -c.

docs.title: Input data
docs.text: Every input is optional in principle, but the force you want decides which ones you need (dependencies). Coordinates are in base pairs on the human reference genome (hg38 chromosome sizes are built in, chromosomes chr1 to chr22).

docs.title: Loops (LOOPS_PATH)
docs.text:
A tab-separated .bedpe file without a header. Each row is one loop:

Column Content 1 chromosome of the first anchor 2, 3 start and end of the first anchor 4 chromosome of the second anchor (not used; loops are assumed intra-chromosomal) 5, 6 start and end of the second anchor 7 loop strength (a count or score; use 1 for single-cell data) 
chr1    160100000   160110000   chr1    160500000   160510000   37.5
chr1    160640000   160650000   chr1    161200000   161210000   12.0

For a region run only loops lying completely inside LOC_START-LOC_END are used. Only the ranking of the strengths matters (Loops). Loops are mandatory unless LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND = False.

docs.title: Compartments (COMPARTMENT_PATH)
docs.text:
Two formats are recognised by the file extension.

CALDER-style .bed (tab-separated, no header): chromosome, start, end and a label in column 4. Labels starting with A.1, A.2, B.1, B.2 give the four subcompartments; plain A and B are also accepted. Rows that overlap the region are used, clipped at its edges.

chr1    160000000   160250000   A.1.1
chr1    160250000   160400000   B.1.2

Signal track .bw / .bigWig, for example a Hi-C eigenvector or a compartment score. The signal is averaged per bead, centred and scaled to \([-1,1]\); higher values are called B and lower values A. Only A and B are distinguished (no subcompartments). Beads with no data stay unassigned.

Short stretches of unassigned beads between annotated ones are filled from their neighbours. The details of how labels are used are in Compartments.

docs.title: Hi-C map (HIC_PATH)
docs.text: A .hic, .cool or .mcool file. The chromosome and region are taken from CHROM, LOC_START and LOC_END, and the map is balanced according to HIC_NORMALIZATION (KR, VC, VC_SQRT or NONE). The resolution of the file does not have to match N_BEADS; the matrix is resized. See Hi-C force.

docs.title: ATAC-seq track (ATACSEQ_PATH)
docs.text: A .bw / .bigWig track, used only by nucleosome interpolation.

docs.title: Gene annotation (GENE_TSV)
docs.text: A table of gene coordinates used to find GENE_NAME or GENE_ID. A hg38 annotation is bundled with the package and is the default.

docs.title: Initial structure (INITIAL_STRUCTURE_PATH)
docs.text: An mmCIF (.cif) file with one bead per atom, used instead of the generated starting structure when BUILD_INITIAL_STRUCTURE = False (Initial structure). The number of beads must equal N_BEADS.

docs.title: Force-field file (FORCEFIELD_PATH)
docs.text: An OpenMM XML file that defines the bead type and its mass. The bundled file is used by default and rarely needs to be changed.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Everything is written below the folder OUT_PATH (default results).

OUT_PATH/
├── model/                 final structures
│   ├── MultiMM_minimized.cif
│   ├── MultiMM_afterMD.cif            (only if SIM_RUN_MD = True)
│   └── chromosomes/                   (genome-wide runs: one file per chromosome)
├── md_frames/             saved frames of the MD trajectory (CIF files)
├── plots/                 diagnostic figures (if SAVE_PLOTS = True)
│   └── chromosomes/
└── metadata/              inputs as seen by the model, validation and logs

docs.title: Structures
docs.text: The 3D models are mmCIF files in which every bead is a particle, so any molecular viewer (ChimeraX, PyMOL, VMD) can open them. MultiMM_minimized.cif is the energy-minimised structure and always exists. MultiMM_afterMD.cif is the last frame of the dynamics. The frames in md_frames/ follow the sampling set by SIM_SAMPLING_STEP or TRJ_FRAMES (Advanced options). In a genome-wide run each chromosome is a separate chain, and also saved as its own file in chromosomes/. Coordinates are in the model units (Units and scales).

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
File Content config_auto.ini the full resolved configuration (defaults, config file, command line and presets) parameters.txt the same parameters as plain text multimm.log, output.log the log of the run MultiMM_init.cif the generated initial structure ms.npy, ns.npy, ds.npy loop anchors (bead indices) and target distances used by the model compartments.npy per-bead compartment states \(s_i\) (Compartments) compartments_from_hic.npy compartments derived from Hi-C PC1, if HIC_BLOCK_COPOLYMER was used chrom_lengths.npy, chrom_idxs.npy chromosome boundaries (in beads) and their order loop_validation.npy how close loop anchors ended up compared with random pairs compartment_validation.npy, compartment_aggregation.npy agreement of the structure with the input compartments, and the 3D clustering of A and B beads hic_validation.npy metrics comparing the structure's contact map with the input Hi-C map MultiMM_compartment_colors.cmd, MultiMM_chromosome_colors.cmd, chimera_gene_coloring.cmd ChimeraX scripts that colour beads by compartment, chromosome or gene

Which of these appear depends on the inputs you used. The .npy files are NumPy arrays: load them with numpy.load.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text: With SAVE_PLOTS = True (default) the plots/ folder holds figures of the structure coloured by compartment or gene, the energy of each force term over the run, and the validation plots (for example the contact map of the structure next to the input map). The exact set depends on which forces and inputs were used.

docs.title: Ensembles
docs.text: With GENERATE_ENSEMBLE = True each run gets its own subfolder run_0, run_1, ..., each with the layout above (Ensembles).

docs.title: Running MultiMM
docs.text:
You run MultiMM by writing a short text file that says what you want (which data, how many beads, which forces) and giving it to the program. Nothing else is needed.

MultiMM is a command-line tool. After installation the command MultiMM is available.

docs.title: The basic command
docs.text:
Describe the run in a config file and pass it with -c:

MultiMM -c config.ini

The result is written to the folder given by OUT_PATH (output). Running MultiMM with no config file uses only the defaults and will stop with an explanation, because some input (at least a loop file, see below) is needed.

docs.title: Overriding values from the command line
docs.text:
Every argument is also a command-line option, written in lower case with two dashes. The command line wins over the config file, which wins over the defaults:

MultiMM -c config.ini --n_beads 2000 --out_path results/test
MultiMM -c config.ini --sim_run_md True

The order is therefore: defaults, then the config file, then the command line. This is convenient for scans, for example looping over --shuffling_seed or --n_beads.

docs.title: What happens during a run
docs.text:
1. Configuration. The arguments are read and checked. A mistyped key in the config file stops the run with a "did you mean ...?" suggestion, and files that are named but do not exist are reported. If MODELLING_LEVEL is set, the preset overwrites some parameters and lists them (Advanced options).
  2. Data loading. Loops, compartments, the Hi-C map and the gene region are read and converted to bead coordinates.
  3. Initial structure. A starting conformation is built, or read from INITIAL_STRUCTURE_PATH (Initial structure).
  4. Force field. The enabled terms are added; a summary table shows which ones are active.
  5. Minimisation. The energy is minimised with OpenMM. This always happens and gives MultiMM_minimized.cif.
  6. Molecular dynamics (only if SIM_RUN_MD = True). Frames are saved along the way.
  7. Validation and plots. The structure is compared with the input data, and diagnostic plots are produced (SAVE_PLOTS).

docs.title: How much it tells you (-v)
docs.text:
By default MultiMM stays quiet: it prints the banner and the eight stages of the pipeline (input data, initial structure, forces, energy minimization, MD simulation, analysis, plotting, outputs), each with a progress bar. Add -v flags when you want to see more.

Flag What you see (none) stages and progress bars only; warnings and errors are always shown -v plus the main messages: what was loaded, which forces were added -vv plus tables of statistics for the input and output data -vvv everything, including debug messages and OpenMM's step-by-step energy report 
MultiMM -c config.ini -vv

Whatever the console level, the full log is written to metadata/multimm.log in your output folder, so nothing is lost. Set NO_COLOR=1 to turn colours off.

docs.title: Checks before you start
docs.text:
MultiMM refuses to run, with a clear message, in these cases:

  • LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND = True (the default!) but no LOOPS_PATH. If you do not have loops, set LE_USE_HARMONIC_BOND = False.
  • HIC_USE_FORCE = True without HIC_PATH.
  • COB_USE_COMPARTMENT_BLOCKS = True without COMPARTMENT_PATH.
  • A path that does not exist.

docs.title: Speed and size
docs.text: The cost grows with the number of beads \(N\) and, for the Hi-C force, with the number of contacted pairs. As rough guidance: a few thousand beads run comfortably on a laptop CPU; tens of thousands benefit from a GPU (PLATFORM = CUDA or OpenCL); the genome-wide preset with 200 000 beads should be run on a GPU and, by default, is only minimised, not simulated. Plots of the heat map are skipped for \(N\ge50\,000\).

docs.title: Examples shipped with the code
docs.text: The folder examples/ of the repository contains ready-to-edit configurations: config_gw.ini (genome-wide) and config_hic.ini (Hi-C-driven region). Copy one, change the file paths and run it with -c.
